clue.text: RAF for instance scrambled above Britain

definitions.note: RAF is a short form standing for Royal Air Force, so it is an example of a shortened name

indicators.note: scrambled eggs are mixed up, so the letters of the two words that follow are jumbled together

explanation.surface: Fighter planes of the Royal Air Force are sent up in a hurry to defend the skies over Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrambled' looks like the RAF's own jargon for an urgent take-off, but it signals an anagram of ABOVE BRITAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Initials such as RAF are a contracted form of a longer name, the classic example of a shortened word or phrase.

clue.text: Send beer outside for missionary

indicators.note: the beer word goes outside, wrapping around the word for send

parts.note: ale is a type of beer
to post a letter is to send it

explanation.surface: An instruction to ship out some beer, as if supplies for a missionary abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: The first Christian missionaries were the twelve disciples sent out by Jesus; the word now means any pioneering preacher.

clue.text: Wicked pupils showing unacceptable behaviour

parts.note: wicked means bad
a form is a class of pupils in a British school

explanation.surface: Naughty schoolchildren misbehaving in class.
explanation.walkthrough: A form is a British school class, so 'pupils' gives FORM.
explanation.definitionFit: Bad form is a British idiom for conduct that breaks social etiquette.

clue.text: From that day forth, on any occasion, wrong at church

parts.note: ever means at any time, on any occasion
a sin is a wrong
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Someone has been behaving badly in church on every occasion since a certain day.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means continuously from a past moment until now, the same idea as from then onwards.

clue.text: Day for teachers producing smaller diagram

definitions.meaning: in Britain an in-service training day, when schools close for staff training, goes by this name
a small picture placed within a larger map or illustration

explanation.surface: A teacher training day spent drawing up a smaller chart.
explanation.walkthrough: British schools close for staff training on what are called INSET days (in-service education and training).
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: the British teacher training day, and a small map set within a bigger one.

clue.text: Such a fish as sinks beneath the waves?

definitions.text: Such a fish as sinks beneath the waves?

parts.words: Such a fish as sinks beneath the waves?
parts.note: the electric ray is a fish with this name, and the same name is given to the underwater missile that sinks ships

explanation.surface: A question about a fish that dives deep under the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sinks' reads as diving, but it means sends ships to the bottom: the weapon is named after the electric ray.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a numbing electric ray and the self-propelled naval weapon that sinks vessels.

clue.text: Pale brown marks in opal here and there with blue

indicators.note: taking letters here and there means every other one
the money letter is placed in the middle of the rest

parts.note: teal is a shade of greenish blue
M stands for marks, the old German currency

explanation.surface: A description of a gemstone, opal, with brown flecks scattered through it and a blue tint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marks' reads as spots on the stone, but it is the old German currency; 'here and there' picks alternate letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The colour is named after ground oats, a light greyish brown.

clue.text: Vigorously mixing liver and eggs say

indicators.note: mixing ingredients stirs them together, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cook energetically stirring liver with eggs, by way of example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like a link meaning 'for example', but its letters are part of the anagram with LIVER and EGGS.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something forcefully and with great energy is a natural sense of the adverb.

clue.text: Dialect good with English whatever it takes?

parts.note: do or die means at any cost, whatever it takes, so the tail of that phrase gives the letters

explanation.surface: A dialect said to be good with English at any cost.
explanation.walkthrough: Geordie is the speech of Tyneside (Newcastle) in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tyneside way of speaking is a well-known regional dialect of England.

clue.text: Standing across river in cloud

indicators.note: the standing word stretches across the river letter, containing it

parts.note: standing means status, one's position in society

explanation.surface: Someone standing on the far side of a river in the mist.
explanation.definitionFit: A low grey layered formation is one of the main types of cloud.

clue.text: Morsel pretty poor for an oceanic bird

indicators.note: poor here means badly done, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A seabird given a pretty poor scrap of food.
explanation.definitionFit: This small petrel lives far out at sea and was thought by sailors to herald bad weather.

clue.text: Commons speeches to omit nothing at first

indicators.note: to omit is to leave out, so a letter is removed
the letter left out sits at the very start of the speeches word

parts.note: orations are formal speeches
O is the figure zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Parliamentary speeches in the House of Commons are told to cut out nothing at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commons' looks like the House of Commons, but it is an old word for shared food allowances.
explanation.definitionFit: Commons are provisions shared out in a college or community, like fixed allowances of food.

clue.text: Excessive about accepting present in addition

indicators.note: accepting means taking something in, so one part goes inside the other
about means turned round, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: OTT is short for over the top, excessive
here means present, as at a roll call

explanation.surface: An excessive gift is offered and accepted on top of everything else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' reads as a gift but means in attendance; 'about' turns the excess word round to TTO before it accepts the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: This formal adverb means besides or as well, relating to what has been mentioned.

clue.text: Second eleven to provide driving force

parts.note: a team of eleven players, as in cricket or football

explanation.surface: A club's second eleven supplies the energy that drives it forward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second eleven' reads as a reserve sports team, but it splits into S and TEAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Steam power drove engines, so the word also means momentum or energy behind something.

clue.text: Fine houses for spymaster of course

indicators.note: to house something is to hold it inside

parts.note: noble means fine, of excellent quality
pro means for, in favour of
M is the head of MI6 in the James Bond stories

explanation.surface: Elegant homes provided for a spy chief, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' looks like the definition but is the container; the definition is 'of course'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are casual replies agreeing readily to a request, meaning certainly or that is easily done.

clue.text: Old man travelling again to arid tableland

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father, one's old man

indicators.note: travelling means moving around, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A father setting off on a journey once more to a dry plateau.
explanation.definitionFit: This region of southern Argentina and Chile is largely dry, windswept steppe and plateau.

clue.text: Very rude about bust?

indicators.note: the rude word goes about, round, the other letter

parts.note: insolent means rude and disrespectful

explanation.surface: Someone extremely coarse about a sculpted bust or a bosom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' suggests a sculpture or a chest; here it means bankrupt.
explanation.definitionFit: To go bust is to go bankrupt, unable to pay one's debts.

clue.text: Slaver statue initially seen has one throwing up?

indicators.note: initially means take the first letter of the word statue

parts.note: a lobber is one who throws a ball high up in the air

explanation.surface: A slave trader sees a statue and is sick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slaver' reads as a slave trader but means to drool; 'throwing up' suggests vomiting but means lobbing.
explanation.definitionFit: To slaver is to let saliva run from the mouth, to dribble.

clue.text: Thai neighbour taken north to a loch by Scotsman

indicators.note: in a down entry, going north means reading upwards, so the letters are reversed

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for loch, a Scottish lake
Ian is a typical Scottish man's name

explanation.surface: Someone from Thailand's neighbour is led north to a Scottish lake by a local man.
explanation.definitionFit: Laos borders Thailand, so a person from Laos is a Thai neighbour.

clue.text: Politician after tea sees winner

indicators.note: the politician comes after the tea in the answer

parts.note: cha is slang for tea
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician who calls after tea sees the victor.
explanation.definitionFit: Champ is short for champion, the victor of a contest.

clue.text: More skilful narrative's opening in Racine novel

indicators.note: the opening letter is put in among the other letters
novel means new, so the letters are made new by rearranging
the opening of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: The start of a story set in a novel by the French dramatist Racine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book, but it rearranges RACINE; the first letter of 'narrative's', N, goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Canny means shrewd or astute, so the comparative means shrewder or cleverer.

clue.text: Feeling love in a room excited American

indicators.note: excited means stirred up, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: US is short for United States, American

explanation.surface: An American in a room, excited by love.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes being full of romantic or sexual desire.

clue.text: Firm into money-changing offers cheapest travel

indicators.note: the firm is put into the other letters
changing means altering, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A company getting into money exchange advertises low-cost trips.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Money-changing' reads as currency exchange, but 'changing' is the anagram signal, giving ENOMY; 'into' puts the firm inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Economy class is the lowest-priced seating on planes and trains.

clue.text: Philistine always knocked over? Goliath finally ducks

indicators.note: in a down entry something knocked over is upended, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: ay is an old word for always

indicators.note: finally means take the last letter

parts.note: a duck is zero in cricket, written O, so two ducks are OO

explanation.surface: David knocks over the Philistine giant Goliath, who at last ducks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Philistine' points at Goliath, the biblical Philistine, but means a lout with no taste for culture.
explanation.definitionFit: A philistine is a person hostile to culture; a yahoo, from Swift's brutish creatures, is a coarse lout.

clue.text: Vessel shooting across the waves?

parts.note: shooting across the waves suggests speeding over the sea, but it also means firing guns from an armed warship

explanation.surface: A boat speeding across the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shooting' seems to mean moving fast, but the boat is literally shooting, with guns.
explanation.definitionFit: A small armed warship used for patrolling or bombarding is named for the guns it carries.

clue.text: Bad-mannered son twice sent back to hospital

indicators.note: sent back means turned round, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a son is a boy
bis is Latin for twice, used for encores and repeats

explanation.surface: A rude son is sent back to hospital twice.
explanation.walkthrough: A yob is British slang for a lout, from BOY reversed; BIS (twice) is a musical instruction to repeat.
explanation.definitionFit: Yob is British slang for a loutish young man, so the adjective means loutish and uncouth.

clue.text: No-one taking part — that's offensive

indicators.note: taking means picking up, so the second piece follows the first

parts.note: no is taken as written and one is the Roman numeral I
some means a part of something

explanation.surface: Nobody joining in, which is taken as an insult.
explanation.definitionFit: Noisome means foul-smelling or disgusting, unpleasant to the senses.

clue.text: Having a turn, our boss reset obsolete browser

definitions.note: a long-extinct dinosaur that browsed on plant leaves

indicators.note: reset means set again in a new arrangement, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The boss takes a turn and resets an outdated web browser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Browser' suggests web software; it is an animal that browses on leaves, and 'obsolete' means extinct.
explanation.definitionFit: This huge long-necked sauropod is extinct and fed by browsing on vegetation.
